utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, you're to begin the presentation of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. There is a matter I'd like to raise both on behalf of myself and indeed of the Prosecution arising out of last week's proceedings, if I may, please. Your Honours will recall the issue that we raised about the torture counts and whether or not you had to deal with those, and Your Honours gave a very, very short oral ruling in relation to those counts. I looked again at the indictment and in particular at paragraph 37, which by reference incorporates within counts 3 to 5 all the other counts, and the phrase that is used is "including those described in paragraphs 43 to 50 below." What the Prosecution and I need to know for the purposes of writing final briefs and making final argument is whether we have to address in those final briefs and documents the counts which follow counts 3 to 5. I hope it isn't me being extremely stupid as a result of Your Honours' ruling last week, and if it is, I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take that into consideration, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I spoke yesterday with the Prosecution and I know they also would seek the same clarification. I turn now to very briefly address you about the nature of the Defence case which will be called on behalf of Dusko Sikirica, but before I do so, can I present the compliments of Mr. Londrovic who is not going to be here until the first break? He apologises for his absence. I'm sure that Your Honours will forgive him for that. The case involving Dusko Sikirica will deal in essence with six different features of the case. The first two witnesses from whom you will hear in the case relate to essentially the issue of conditions within Keraterm camp. The first two witnesses will deal with in particular the provision of food at Keraterm, how that was done, where the food came from and the nature of that food. There will then be a group of witnesses who come from the hospital in Prijedor. Most of those are going to give evidence without any form of protection at all. They deal with the period in August 1992 when, as has been asserted, Dusko Sikirica ceased to have any connection with Keraterm, that taking place at the end of July 1992, and was assigned to guarding duties at Prijedor hospital. And you will hear from a number of witnesses who deal with Dusko Sikirica's presence at Prijedor hospital and, in particular, how they are able to fix the date when he arrived because he was responsible physically for bringing into the hospital a particular piece of equipment. You will then deal with a single witness who, like some of the Prosecution witnesses, was a detainee in Keraterm camp but at the very beginning, at the very opening of that camp, someone who was there for a number of days and one of those who was released from Prijedor camp, having been interrogated by the authorities. There will then be three character witnesses who will deal with the character of Dusko Sikirica, how they knew him from some considerable time ago, and in particular, they will deal with his attitude towards members of other ethnic groups, other nationalities, in Bosnia before the war and before the change in political life took place. There will then be a single witness who deals with an allegation made by an early witness in the Prosecution case, an allegation that Dusko Sikirica casually shot somebody close to the weigh hut, he having just received goods from a friend of his, and it is the friend from whom you will hear. And the Defence say that in relation to that particular witness, it not only raises a reasonable doubt as to the taking place of that alleged murder, but we say demonstrates that it simply did not happen at all. Finally, there will be two witnesses, the first of whom who will deal with the assignment of Dusko Sikirica and others to the checkpoint, of which we have heard somewhat in the case, the checkpoint at Hambarine. The witness is a former reserve police officer who at the time, May 1992, was responsible for maintaining rosters in relation to what work was to be done by each individual reserve police officer working out of Prijedor II police station. The second aspect with which he will deal will be the issue of the assignment of Dusko Sikirica to Keraterm, and in particular, what duties, what powers he had upon his assignment to that place. Further, he will deal with the individual about whom we have heard in the case during the Prosecution's case, Zivko Knezevic, and how he was in command of Prijedor II police station and how, in effect, he kept in his hands control of all meaningful matters in relation to Keraterm. Having spoken very briefly to the Prosecution yesterday and today, I anticipate that the first group of witnesses may well go quite quickly, and that will take us -- those are what I would call the conditions and hospital witnesses, and so it's possible we may finish slightly early this week. Our next group of witnesses arrives at the weekend. So it may be that that's slightly bad planning by me, but I anticipate that we in fact will finish probably by close of business on Friday of next week, I would hope. I hope that's of use to Your Honour. I call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, before my friend calls his first witness, I do believe there is an outstanding motion with respect to protective measures, and I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is, and I'm grateful to my learned friend for reminding me, and I had completely forgotten that. Your Honour, before the witness comes in, there is an application in respect of her to have protection in the following way: that she be granted a pseudonym, that she be able to give her evidence subject to both face and voice distortion. Your Honour, you have the summary indicating what she did and what work she did. She is extremely apprehensive as to the potential consequences of being identified as someone who worked in Keraterm at one of its most Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. difficult parts of its history, and for those reasons she has requested that she be granted the measures which are sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Needless to say, the Prosecution agrees that, where appropriate, protective measures ought to be granted. We, in fact, have been requesting protective measures where we deemed it was important as well. My only concern is whether or not there is a need for voice distortion, and although I take no position on whatever appropriate measures the Court may deem to be necessary in order to protect the identity of witnesses, I just do not know whether in these instances voice distortion is a requirement. That may depend on the circumstances in each individual case. I'm not here to question my friend as to what the particular issues are, but that may be something that the Court may want to make an inquiry about. I do not oppose. I simply raise the question as to whether or not, other than a pseudonym and facial distortion, we need to actually go into voice distortion as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has been the run-of-the-mill protection; pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct, including Prosecution witnesses, and we have tried to minimise the -- not minimise, but provide adequate protection and yet to have the proceedings as open as possible. As I say, I'm not opposing. I do not want to be opposing. I'm raising the issue as to the necessity of voice distortion, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The objective of protective measures, in part, is to allow the witness to feel that when they come here, that they are comfortable in the knowledge that they will be protected by the Tribunal, and each witness whom we were able to see down in Prijedor had explained to them what measures are available. And in each case, the request of the witnesses is that which has been placed before you as to what they felt comfortable with which would enable them to come here and give evidence. I note that it's not an objection by the Prosecution in respect of this witness. That is how she felt comfortable enough to come here and give evidence; in the knowledge that she could have those protective measures granted to her. On the second point, I make this observation: The Defence have a large number of witnesses for whom no protection is sought at all, probably a greater proportion of its witnesses than the Prosecution, and so, yes, there is a considerable openness in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will grant the protection in the terms sought.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness pseudonym will be DA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm not expecting this witness. I'm expecting a female witness with this name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can we, for the purposes of establishing her name, please go into -- very briefly into closed session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DA, I'd like to ask you, please, about your employment from August 1987. In August 1987, did you commence work at a factory in Prijedor called Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when you commenced work at Keraterm, what job were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in May 1992, did you -- were you still working in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you recall the period when armed clashes, fighting, began in Prijedor in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When the fighting started, did you remain at work or was there a period when you did not go to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: For several days, we did not go to work. The morning when it started to happen, they came for us to take us along so that we could go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DA, how -- who was it who came to ask you to go along to go back to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: My boss came, and Mirko Mudrinic, and a man called Dzelalija.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what was the name of your boss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you returned to work at Keraterm, had detainees by that time arrived at the facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, there were already detainees there. We were offered to work again to prepare food for these detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you help us about this; when you first returned to work, were you able to assess how many detainees were present at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Because this was at the very beginning, there weren't that many of them. I couldn't tell you exactly, but there would have been about 100 men. I couldn't tell you exactly. I did not know the exact count.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you engaged in serving food to those detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And from where did the food come that you served to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: At first, that is the first two or three days, we prepared some food ourselves. However, later on, as the number of arrivals grew, we could no longer prepare the food because we did not have capabilities for that, so from the mining cafeteria, food was transported to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After a few days, did the number of detainees at Keraterm increase? And if so, can you estimate to what number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I don't know the exact number. We distributed the food that arrived. The number of detainees did grow but I did not know exactly how many did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The food which came from outside Keraterm, how was it transported? Can you tell us that, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know. Probably by van. Some men would bring the food to the door. I think that there were some men in a van. I don't know, they probably were military. In any case, they would bring it to us and leave it there and then we would distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in what sort of containers did the food arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The food arrived in thermos containers. It was hermetically sealed; in other words, it was protected from losing its heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when it arrived, was it taken to the canteen or taken somewhere else at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: At the entrance to the kitchen, the entrance we used to go in, we had some tables there, and that's where we put the food; and they would come there, stand in a queue, approach us, take food, and go to eat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DA, I'd like you to look, please, at I think it's Prosecution Exhibit 2, some photographs of Keraterm. Would you first of all just look through the bundle of photographs that is being placed in front of you, and if you can find a photograph where the site from which the food was distributed is shown, could you then ask for that to be put on the ELMO, which is to your left. If you look through, there are other photographs which may show it better.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could you put the microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Right. Would you put that, please, onto -- the usher will put it onto the ELMO, and if you could then use the pointer to indicate on that photograph where the food was served, please. You have to point to the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It's here, inside, when you go through the door. We were inside and they were outside. They were outside, and we distributed food to them and they would go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you able to examine the quality of the food which you were serving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The quality was medium quality. It was neither bad food nor especially good food. For the conditions prevailing at the time, it was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And could you describe to us, Witness DA, please, what type of food, what sort of food it was, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It was food cooked in a big pot, so it was cooked food. And it was quite thin. In our part of the world, when you cook in a big pot, it's a kind of stew, and it contained vegetables, macaroni, rice, cabbage, whatever. That's the way we cook in our part of the world: food like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did it contain any meat; and if so, was it every day that it contained meat or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. There wasn't a lot. There was small pieces of meat, but there was some.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you describe the process by which each detainee would receive his meal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: They would come there, stand in a queue, and they would take the food one by one. We poured it into bowls for them. And the bread was cut up, so they would take some bread and take a bowl and go outside and eat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You described bread being served to them. How much bread was served to each detainee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, while I was there - because I wasn't working there the whole time - they could take two or three slices each, depending on how much they asked for. Afterwards, I don't know what it was like, because I wasn't there all the time, but while I was there, they could take as much bread -- well, two or three slices. That's how much we would give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DA, how long did you remain at Keraterm doing this particular job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Approximately 20 days, not more, and then I asked my boss to release me because I had some problems at home, so she let me go and then a colleague of ours who used to work with us continued working with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've spoken earlier of the conditions prevailing at the time. Were there, over the summer period, May to August 1992, were there food shortages in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What sort of commodities were notably in short supply in Prijedor over that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, we used what we had at home. We couldn't go out much in the beginning. And then, later on, it was more normal. It was possible to get food if one had money. If one had money, one could get everything. But in the beginning, well, we had to find ways to manage because we couldn't go about much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you aware of detainees receiving any other food from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. They could have food brought to them, and somebody probably received that food and distributed it to them. I don't know exactly, but I do know that at the time I was there at the beginning, they were able to get food from outside. Later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And how did you become aware that detainees were able to receive food from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: From friends, from those who received food. They would even ask me to tell a neighbour to bring some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you pass those requests on, as you had been asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did those people, as far as you know, then bring food to the people who had requested it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I personally didn't see it, but I think they did. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the period that you were working at Keraterm, that you've described, serving food to detainees, were you able also to see anything of the water supply at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: At that time, there was water. They had water in the compound, a tap. The water supply was normal. If there were water shortages, then water was brought in in tank trucks, so there was water. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were engaged in distributing food to the detainees, how long did that process take each day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: At the very beginning, while I was working there, I would work for two or three hours at a time. That's how long I would spend there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were there ever occasions when there was insufficient food for all the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, maybe, because people were arriving all the time, brought in in buses, so it was possible that someone was left without food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If there was a problem of any kind in relation to your job, to whom would you speak in order to resolve that problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I spoke to my boss. She was the only one I could turn to. There was no one else I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And help me about this, please, Witness DA: Do you know or did you know at the time, a man called Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. I never knew anyone personally. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DA, would you wait there, please, and answer any questions from my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Defence may come first before the Prosecution. We admire my learned friend's enthusiasm for the job but she must wait, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Any cross-examination, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mrs. DA, during your testimony, when answering the questions put to you by my learned colleague Mr. Greaves, you mentioned that only during the first few days did you prepare food in Keraterm. Afterwards, it was brought from the canteen in the mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what the mine canteen was; where it was, what it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: In our town, the mine canteen was a socially-owned enterprise where the miners used to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How far is that from the Keraterm camp compound, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, it's perhaps a kilometre or a kilometre and a half, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could we say that the mine canteen was in the centre of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Answering the questions put to you by Mr. Greaves, you said that when the war broke out, you had only what you had at home to eat, but later on, if one had money, one could buy food. Could you tell us, that period that you described as the beginning, when you were using the stores you had at home, can you tell us how long this period lasted? For example, starting in May or June 1992 until when? When could we say that this period ended and that supplies became more regular or better organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. How long? How much time passed? Well, I think it wasn't long. It wasn't long, but I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In answer to the question about water, since you worked in Keraterm even before this period, that is May 1992, could you please tell us, in the factory compound, in the Keraterm building - I'm talking about the building now - the taps that existed in the building, the water flowing from these taps, was it fit for drinking? Was it drinkable water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I think it was. We didn't have any other kind of water. We had a tap in the compound which was used, and probably in the dormitories. I didn't go inside there, but it was all normal, potable water.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you drink this water too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, because we were working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said, in answer to questions, that in the period while you were working there in Keraterm, people arrived every day, fresh numbers of people arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the distribution of food? Was it always the detainees from the same room who queued up for the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that when people arrived -- I don't know whether it was always the same people. I'm not sure. I think that as they arrived, they stood in the queue to receive food. And whether there was some sort of system where it was fixed, I don't think so. I don't really know, but I don't think there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the small room that you showed us on the photograph where you were and from where you distributed food, was there a bread-slicing machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but we didn't use it much because there were power cuts sometimes, so we would slice the bread by hand. And in the beginning, while there weren't many people, we sliced it by hand, using a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When the number of people increased, did any of the detainees help you to cut bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: While I was working there -- well, maybe later on, after I left, but in the beginning, there were the two of us and there was no need. Then probably later on, when there were more people, when my colleague came to work, then probably that happened, but while I was there, there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And one brief question to finish: When we were talking about the miners' canteen in the centre of town of Prijedor, from where food arrived, that mining canteen, did it belong to the Keraterm plant or did it belong to some other company or enterprise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, it belonged to the mine, and that's where they prepared food for their employees. We did not have anything to do with them. We had our food and they prepared food for their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The mine canteen, did it belong to the Omarska mine? I'm talking -- sorry, the Ljubija, the Ljubija iron ore mine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had their own kitchen in Omarska, and this was there for their employees working in town, working in offices in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. I have finished, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, with respect to the food that you were providing to the detainees for the 20 or so days that you were at Keraterm, can you tell us if that food came every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Court, if you remember, whether the water that was brought from time to time at the camp, whether it was plentiful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I think there was water. I think there was enough. I don't know, but I think there was enough water. We had enough while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself also drink the same water that was available for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you remember, [redacted] [redacted] can you tell us the length of time that the detainees had to eat the food that was provided to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, we stayed there -- well, probably as the numbers grew, we stayed there until about 3.00, approximately, so they had probably 15 or 20 minutes to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness DA, you told Mr. Ostojic that you drank the same water as the detainees. Did you eat the same food as the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could eat it. We could eat the same food as they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. My question was: Did you eat the same food as the detainees, not whether you could eat it. ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DA, did the guards in the camp eat the same food as the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It's the case, Witness DA, that the detainees were fed only once per day. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because food arrived only once a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You indicated in your evidence that when you first began distributing the food, there were about 100 detainees in the camp and that there was an increase. Would you say that that increase was a dramatic increase in the number of detainees who arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, it grew day by day. I couldn't tell you exactly. I didn't know much about it, but the number did increase, yes. Sometimes more, sometimes less, but it did increase.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many detainees would you estimate were in the camp at the time you left, that is, on the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, in my estimation, there were probably about 300 or 400 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Is it the case that the amount of food to be distributed did not increase in accordance with the number of detainees who were brought into the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that as they arrived, it's possible that when there wasn't enough food -- it's possible that such a thing happened if, after the meal, people were brought in or -- I don't know. But mostly care was taken that they would be provided with a meal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sometimes the food ran out and detainees, some detainees, didn't receive any food during a day; that's correct, isn't it, Witness DA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't know, but it could have happened. It's possible. Probably, as I said, if -- if they arrived after the meal when we had gone home already or if someone was brought in afterwards, then it's possible that they were left without food, but they could get food. They could have it brought to them. They could receive food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say "they could have it brought to them," you mean they could have it brought to them from people outside the camp? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. They could receive it from one of their own, if that was an issue. Yes, they could receive that food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've indicated, Witness DA, that there was a line, a queue, of detainees who would come to you and you would distribute the food. It's the case, isn't it, that sometimes all of those in the line would not receive food, the food would run out before the line was completed? That's the case, isn't it, Witness DA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: While I worked there, that did not happen, but I don't know what was happening after I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The food, would you agree, could be described as a watery soup? Would you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. The food was not especially good but it was not watery either. It was of medium quality, given the circumstances, and in those circumstances, it was regular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness DA, what do you mean by "given the circumstances"? What circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean what happened there. There were people -- that is, given the circumstances for cooking for such people. It was regular. It wasn't of extra quality but I think it was all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean, then, given the circumstances in which the detainees found themselves at Keraterm? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You began to distribute this food shortly after the camp was established, so that you were able to observe the first arrivals, so to speak, in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you observed these men over a period of 20 days; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you notice that the men were losing weight and losing weight dramatically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: You know something, the environment in which we were, I myself was losing weight by simply observing what was going on around me, in the environment that we found ourselves in, the circumstances under which we lived, of course. We were all losing weight. I too lost weight while working there, and while observing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You, of course, were able to eat when you were outside the camp as well; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Of course, when I would come home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The detainees were in a dirty and unkept state; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I think that there was enough water for them to wash. I think that was provided for them. I did not observe that -- that they were especially dirty. I think that that was not the case, because there was enough water.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Witness DA, that the detainees appeared to you to be in a clean state? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, again, given the circumstances there, of course, I mean they were not especially dirty. They did not work either. They were just held there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Insofar as the state of the detainees is concerned, what significance do you attach to the fact that they did not work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I mean they simply stayed there. They had enough water to wash if they needed to. I believe that there was no need for them to be dirty. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The question I asked you is: Were they, in fact, dirty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. According to me, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DA, did you observe any injuries on any of the detainees whom you served?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It did happen when they arrived that one could see some bruises on some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "when they arrived"? Arrived where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: When they arrived at Keraterm, when they appeared, I did observe that some of them had some bruises on their faces or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were, in fact, serving this food from inside this kitchen area; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes -- no. It was -- we placed tables outside so that they could approach us more easily to take food, because the kitchen was on the top floor. We had to go downstairs so that we would be closer to them, to distribute it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the circumstances in which you able to observe these detainees were such that you -- they were in the line, queueing up for food, and you were serving them the food; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So how was it that you were able to tell that these detainees whom you say were bruised had -- were recent arrivals in the camp? How could you tell that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I did not see them on that day, but I would see them the next day, and I would see that some of them had some bruises perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You indicated that -- I think you said they had 15 minutes to consume their food. Isn't it the case, Witness DA, that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: -- they had a lot less time than that? They, in fact, had a very tight time limit and they would be taken out of the line and beaten while they were queueing for food; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I did not see that. It did not happen in front of me so that I really did not observe that. I don't know that anybody did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: But you were able to observe the line of detainees who were queueing, weren't you, Witness DA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you saying that you never saw any of the detainees taken out of the line and beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of the guards at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. They were in camouflage uniforms. They were wearing sunglasses. I did not know these men at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you ever observe a guard who had long hair and carried a baseball bat and was referred to as Cupo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. They were around, but I really did not know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I knew him because he lived near us. [redacted] [redacted] But no, I did not notice him. I simply did not pay much attention to who was there, what, but I did know him from before, from the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DA, Zoran Zigic would come to the camp and take people out of the food queue and beat them. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I may have met him accidentally in passing when we would come in, but I did not see him doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "I may have met him accidentally"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: When we would come to work, we saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was he doing when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't know that either, what he did. I would come, do my job, and did not see what anyone was doing really. I wasn't interested in that. It was their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to observe what was going on in the camp, didn't you, Witness DA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I did have an opportunity, but I came to do my work, and when we would finish it, we would go home, so that I really don't know what went on there. While we worked, nothing happened; and after that, I don't know. In front of us, while we worked there, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Why do you say that you don't know what happened afterwards? Do you suspect that something happened to the prisoners or the detainees after you left? Is that why you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't know. I really cannot tell you anything. I did not see anything that I can tell you about, and I don't know about other things. I cannot tell you about things that I don't know; I just cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It was very hot at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And your evidence is that there was one tap, apart from the water tank, to service the detainees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: They were in rooms. I imagine they had water there. I never entered those rooms. But I know that there was a tap on the perimeter, and I really cannot tell you anything else. I did not enter those rooms to see what they had in there. That was not part of my job, so I cannot tell you anything about that. My job was to distribute food and to go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: If you didn't enter the rooms, why do you say that you imagine there was a tap in there or there was water in the rooms, if you didn't go into the rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, probably if they had water -- I don't know. As I said, I never entered there. I don't know. I know that there was water. I cannot say that they didn't have water, but I did not enter there, so I don't know what they had in there. I know that there was enough water. On the perimeter there was water. Anybody could use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You don't know, Witness DA, what access or what permission the detainees had to access that tap, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: That I really don't know. As I said, I went there to do my work. When I would finish, I would go home, and I don't know what else was going on and who was doing it, who was in charge of it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DA, would you accept a proposition that you turned a blind eye to what was going on in the camp? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I said that I did not have an opportunity to do anything. I wanted to go home. And of course, I also did not have a wish to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: A wish to do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I did not have interest to go in there to look who had water, whether they had it or not, because I assumed that it was somebody else's job. I did my job and went home, so that I really cannot tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You indicated that if you had problems, you would speak to your boss. Did you have occasion to do that during the time that you were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you ever say to your boss that the numbers of detainees were increasing but there was a shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, she worked alongside with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness DA, that at the same time the Keraterm detention camp was operating, the Omarska detention camp was operating? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I only heard of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know where the food came from that was taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just pardon me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DA, you had no control over how the prison -- how the detainees were taken from their rooms or called from their rooms and allowed to queue for the food, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So you don't know whether some of the detainees were left in their rooms without food, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't know that, no, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know any of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Some I did know from the company where I used to work. Some I knew from sight. There were a lot of people that I knew, because we would pass by each other. We lived in the same town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So you know, Witness DA, that there were only Muslims and Croats detained there; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you, Witness DA, fear some retaliation from the Serbs at home for testifying here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I think that I have nothing to fear. I did nothing -- I think that I only did some good by distributing food, and if that is a sin, to feed someone, that is, then I would have reason for fear. As it is, I don't. I think that I have no reason to fear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no re-examination. Do any of Your Honours have questions for the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness DA, that concludes your testimony and you are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to suggest starting the break slightly early and finishing it slightly early, and then -- rather than just having a few words from the witness and then breaking it off. Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We will take the break and resume at 25 minutes after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the next witness, there is an application of exactly the same nature as the last witness, and I would ask that she be granted those measures of protection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but please outline the grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. What I've indicated is the grounds are the same as the last witness's. She too, having had explained to her the basis upon which protection could be granted, indicated that she wished to have protection. She was concerned about potential repercussions if she was identified as having been in any way part of the arrangements at Keraterm during 1992, whether it be from her own community or from the other communities that were involved in the conflict in Prijedor in 1992. And having had the measures explained to her, she indicated that she would feel comfortable, only feel comfortable, if she had the benefit of pseudonym, face distortion, and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see that there is no objection from the Prosecution. The measures are granted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for the witness will be DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we please go into closed session briefly while I establish her name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When did you start working at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. I worked in the Electrokeramika complex in Ljubija, in Prijedor, in Selena, and at Keraterm. So we passed from one plant to another, and it was all a single company, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Approximately when did you start working at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, I worked there for about three years, I think, but I can't tell you the date or the year. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you still working at Keraterm in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When the armed fighting -- the fighting started in the Prijedor area in May 1992, did there come a time when you ceased to go temporarily to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And for how long did that period last when you stopped going to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Two or three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And when you next returned to Keraterm, had the function of Keraterm by now changed from being a factory into being a place where people were being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you returned for the first time after this period, can you say approximately how many detainees were there upon your return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Up to a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was it your job at that time to distribute food to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Would you go to Keraterm every day in order to carry out that function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And on each day, at what time would you go to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, approximately from 2.00 until we finished, and it lasted for three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The food which was distributed to the detainees, was that cooked on the premises or was it brought in from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: It wasn't cooked on the premises. It was brought in, I think from the mining company canteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And in what sort of containers was the food brought in to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, it was sort of thermos flask but very, very big.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: During your period when you worked distributing food at Keraterm, did you receive any pay from the company which was -- which had formerly run the Keraterm factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was it your normal salary or was -- were you paid in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Normal salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many -- apart from yourself, how many other people were engaged in distributing the food to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: When I was there, there was another woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Apart from the food in the containers which you have described, was there any bread provided to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And was that in the form of ordinary loaves that were sliced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were the loaves sliced at Keraterm or did they come ready-sliced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We cut them in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say, "We cut them," was that you and your colleague or did the detainees have anything to do with it, or was there a machine? Help us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We did have a machine. When there was power, we used the machine. When there was no electricity, four of the detainees helped us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the food distributed from: inside the building or outside the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: In front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And can you help us about this: Did the detainees form a queue in order to receive their food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did they have a bowl or did you give them a bowl of any kind, or a plate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We had our factory bowls from our canteen. They would take them and then stand in a queue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The food which you served to the detainees, can you describe, please, what the quality of that food was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, it was of medium quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What typically would the food contain in terms of ingredients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, it was the usual kind of stew that's normally eaten in our area. There would be beans or string beans or cabbage one day, paprikas, potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And would the stew contain meat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And would there be meat in the stew every day, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: If I can just return briefly to the bread. Where did the bread come from that was distributed to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: From our town bakery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you recall if the food which you were serving was also served to the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: During the time when the detainees were in a queue, waiting to get their food, did you ever observe any mistreatment of any prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were there ever any occasions when the food ran out before the queue had come to an end so that some detainees didn't get fed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How often would that happen, and can you say why it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: It didn't happen very often. It happened sometimes when new people arrived and they had -- their arrival hadn't been planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The other person who was working with you, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you help us, please: Was there water connected and available at Keraterm during the period when you were there in that summer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. When there was water from the town water supply, it could be used. Sometimes that water ran out and then water was brought in by tank trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you able to observe detainees using water from where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, we know from other evidence in the case that the Keraterm facility closed around the 5th of August, 1992. Did you continue up until the time when it ceased to be used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did the process of food distribution and water availability, did that continue until that time, 5th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Would you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Petrovic or Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Madam, Witness DB, I have only a few brief questions for you. You said that food was transported, as you said, from "our mining company canteen." Did this belong to the Keraterm company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No. It belonged to the Ljubija iron ore company.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether, during the time you were working in Keraterm, there were frequent power cuts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In those situations, I assume that, as you said, the bread-slicing machines could not operate, so detainees came to help; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In situations when there was a power cut, was there water in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: When there's no electricity, there's no water either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what the detainees used to eat out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The plastic bowls that we used to serve soups to our employees in the canteen, soup bowls.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So these bowls were used before the detainees arrived in the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who told you, who spoke to you, telling you to come to work in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I was called to go to work by my boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that the woman you were working with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The job you did in Keraterm distributing food, was that your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we say, then, that on the wartime conditions, you were actually mobilised to do this job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, in a manner of speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. Your Honours, that completes my examination, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Rodic. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Witness DB, I'm going to ask you a series of questions. With respect to the slicing of the bread that you testified to, I think you told us that bread was sliced by you, your boss, as well as four other detainees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at any time when the detainees were slicing the bread, did you instruct them on what size to slice each piece of bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone instruct you as to what size to slice the bread from the loaves that you were cutting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you, as well as the four detainees and your boss, were slicing this loaf of bread for the detainees as you would normally in your home before and after June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you with respect to the food that was served at the camp. You mentioned that the food was also served to the guards, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, not that food. They received food from the same canteen but in smaller containers, other containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to receive the food, you just separated a canteen, a thermos full of the same food that the detainees were eating and segregated that in a separate section of the camp, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: That was done by the driver who brought the food. He would leave what was for the guards at the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who would order the food for the detainees as well as the guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the guards at any time ordered the foods -- the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the basis of that? Why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, I think they had no influence, just as I had no influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Witness DB, that, in fact, neither you nor the guards had any authority in terms of ordering food for any of the detainees or people involved in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you, Witness DB, whether or not you had the authority to order the food, such as from the place that you're ordering the food, the type of food that was being ordered. You had no authority to do that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also true that the guards didn't have authority to decide where the food would be ordered from, the type of food that would be brought in, or how much food would be brought in, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: They couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The water that you spoke of at the camp, did you drink any of the water there at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you drank the same water that the detainees drank, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DB, did you eat the food, the same food, as the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I didn't need to. I stayed there only for three or four hours, and then I went home to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were simply employed as a person to distribute the food, correct? That was the extent of your involvement or employment at the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How is it that you know what the authority of the guards in the camp was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, I had occasion to see. If there was one kind of food for the detainees, they had the same kind of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'll just ask the question again. How is it that you know what the guards' authority was as concerns the ordering of the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I asked, "Can the amount be increased?" And they would say they had no authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you asked that question because clearly there was not enough food to go around; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, it would happen sometimes that there wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you also work in the Omarska detention camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When was it that you -- are you able to put a date on when you started at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was around, well, some 20 days after the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And at that time, that is when you started, you say there were a thousand or so detainees at the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I said up to a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you left, that is when the camp closed, how many detainees would you say - just an estimate - were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I don't know that. Maybe over a thousand, a little over a thousand, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you worked, I think you said, from 2.00 p.m. for two to three hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You didn't have much time to serve each detainee, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: We had enough time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Enough time to do precisely what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Enough time to pour the food, to hand them bread, and we didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: They only received one slice of bread per day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No. Sometimes two, three, depending on the amount of bread we received.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were serving the food from outside the building, and so you had, I suggest to you, ample opportunity to observe the prisoners or the detainees as they lined up or as they queued for food. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Well, we had an opportunity but we didn't have time to observe them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness DB, the detainees were taking the food from you right in front of your face, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At that time, you had, I suggest to you, ample opportunity to observe the state they were in; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Detainees were in a filthy and unkept state, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And they had -- some of them had obvious injuries on their bodies. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the detainees had obviously lost a lot of weight. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes. That was to be expected. They were in a prison and they only received one meal per day. It affects your mental state. And I also lost weight myself while working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The detainees lost a lot of weight; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you -- you were in the camp on the 1st of July, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you've given some evidence that you spoke at times to the guards at the camp. Did you know the names of the guards, or any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Cupo Banovic, with long hair, who carried a baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know a guard by the name of Kondic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, Cupo Banovic removed some of the prisoners or some of the detainees from the food line and beat those detainees. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you see Cupo Banovic on the 20th of July beat some of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were there on that date; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: While I was there, nothing happened. There was no mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to observe a Muslim priest who was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to see people who were there, but I did not know who was what there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In late July, a group of detainees from the Brdo region were brought to the camp. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And those men were placed into Room 3. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And those detainees were not given any food or water for a number of days. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How do you say those detainees from Room 3 received their food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The first three days they did not come out, but the food would be brought to their door.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Who took the food to the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Some of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what quantity of food was taken to the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The same as to the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know whether those detainees actually ate that food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you were aware of the presence of those detainees in Room 3 and that they didn't come out for several days. Do you recall an occasion when they were brought out and made to lie face down in the sun for a number of hours one afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were in the camp from 2.00 until approximately 5.00 p.m. every day. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were in the camp on the day before the Room 3 massacre, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you saw a machine-gun, at least one machine-gun, facing toward Room 3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I did not observe that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: He was in the camp frequently, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: That is where I saw him. I personally did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did you see him doing in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, he must have been doing something while he was there. What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: As I said, nothing in particular. I saw him walking around the perimeter, but I didn't see him doing anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no -- oh, I do have one question in re-examination. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DB, you've spoken about the food and were asked about the food which was served to the guards. Can you help me about this, please: Was the food which was served to the guards, did that come from the same containers which had the food for the detainees or from different containers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I told you that it was the same type of containers, only smaller in size.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But the food which was in the smaller containers, that was the same food which was in the large containers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: I believe so because it was the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions. Do Your Honours have any questions for the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Witness DB, that concludes your testimony and you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go briefly into private session whilst I outline the application in respect of protective measures for this witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go briefly into private session so I might establish his identity, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DC, in May 1992, can you tell us, please, what your occupation was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you, please, about the 30th of May 1992. Were you working on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 30th of May 1992, I was on duty in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, at what time did you start work on the 30th of May, or if it was a shift that had started the day before, when you started the day before, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: That was a shift that started on the evening of the 29th at 1900 hours, and it lasted until the 0700 hours of the 30th. At least, that was supposed to have been the end of that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you, please, about the period at 4.40 in the morning. Were you engaged in your duties away from the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you driving an ambulance at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. That morning, I was in the hospital. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you used the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was told there was no translation of the question, in fact. During the course of your duty that night, did you have occasion to use the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning, around four -- 4.40 a.m., I received a call, and I was to go to the centre of town. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The ambulance that you used, did it bear red cross markings on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, they had all the markings of a professional ambulance. It had the lights, it had rotation lights, it had the red cross signs on the sides, and they were clearly marked as an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And at that time in the morning, was it already light?
