utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, it had already dawned. That was 20 to 5.00 on May the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this, please: Did you carry out the job which you had been sent to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No, I did not carry out the job, because halfway to the location I was attacked by - how shall I put it - a group of extremists, which fired on me from firearms while I was in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, let's just take that in stages, please. Whereabouts were you when this attack took place? What part of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I was under the overpass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you moving at the time when the attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. The vehicle was moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At what speed was the vehicle moving when the attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: It was moving at approximately 40 kilometres per hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The people who attacked you, were they in front of your vehicle or behind it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. They were to the left and right of my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you able to observe them before the attack commenced or as the attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I observed them before the attack commenced, when I was coming downhill towards the overpass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As you approached them, were you able to see if the people on either side of the road were armed in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I saw them, because the group was crossing. In fact, I disrupted them, their crossing the road, and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DC, were you able to identify what type of weapons these people were armed with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I could not recognise the weapons as such, but I saw that they were armed with automatic rifles. But I couldn't tell you what make those automatic rifles were. I just saw them with those type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did there come a time when members of the group fired at your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, at the moment when I arrived, when I was just -- when I had reached the pillars, just under the overpass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was it all the members of the group or just a few of them who fired at your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Most of those who were there shot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: First of all, was your vehicle hit by the fire which was directed at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. The vehicle was hit by several bullets. In fact, it was riddled with bullets, and the windshield was broken and the side windows. The doors were also shot through, and the back door as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At this time, were you wounded by any of the bullets which entered the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. Several bullets wounded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Whereabouts in your body were you hit at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I was hit in both legs, both arms, the chest, neck; lower arm, upper arm, lower leg, upper leg, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, at this time, were you able to keep control of the vehicle, or did you lose control of the vehicle in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: At that moment while the fire was going on, the left arm and the right leg were shot. I lost control of them. But I kept the steering wheel with my left arm. I was also grazed in the left forearm. And as the vehicle was moving and as it had momentum, it just kept going uphill. It went up and it came to a stop above the overpass, but they kept on shooting after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you injured again as a result of the continued shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: They fired shots behind me, and when I came out, they continued shooting after me, when I passed through the underpass, and then I had some entry/exit wounds in my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you able to recover control of the vehicle or did you lose consciousness at any stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I didn't lose consciousness straight away, not there. I tried to move the vehicle toward the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you able, eventually, to drive from the immediate scene where you had been attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I moved forward twice in the direction of the SUP, hoping that there would be someone there to give me assistance, because there was no one in the street I could turn to. It lasted a long time, because I lost consciousness twice. The second time -- the last time I lost consciousness I stayed there longer, and from there they, after a time, transported me to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back to the passage of your vehicle as you approached and then passed the group of people who attacked you. As you passed the group of people, how close were they to the vehicle as you passed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: They were a metre away, or a metre and a half, on the pavement. They were standing on the pavement, on both sides of the road. So the ones on the right-hand side were about a metre away, or a metre and a half, and the ones on the left-hand side were the width of the road away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you were standing a metre away from your vehicle, would the markings on that vehicle be clearly visible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: The markings on an ambulance are clearly visible from a far greater distance, and especially as my rotating light was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a result of your injuries, were you detained in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I had enormous consequences, because I was taken to Banja Luka from Prijedor, and then from Banja Luka to Belgrade the same day, because I was very seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness DC, we don't want to see your injuries, but please would you be so kind as to describe what injuries you received, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I was wounded in the right arm, in the lower arm, in the right shoulder, the right side of my chest, my right leg. My right leg was seven centimetres off. It was ripped apart. That was above the knee, my thigh. Then I was also wounded in my left thigh, my left arm, and my neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long did you spend in hospital before you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I spent 18 months in various hospitals in Belgrade, until I was taken back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At the present time, have you been assessed, as it were, as to the degree of invalidity that you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a 90-per-cent permanent invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to this incident taking place, had you been engaged in duties as [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Wounded people? Where? I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the days immediately before you were injured, had you been engaged in duties as [redacted], people who had been wounded in the fighting, anywhere in Prijedor or in the Prijedor district?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: At that time, there were no wounded people in Prijedor. There had been no fighting in those days. On the 30th of May, in the morning, that's when that started happening in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you carry any of those wounded people or any wounded people on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. I set out because I had received the call and I had set out to the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know if people were injured and wounded that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I do. I heard that 18 people were killed and 35 or 36 wounded on that day, after that, or rather after I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: People were talking about it in the hospital, everywhere, and it was in the newspapers. The medical staff, the hospital staff, said that there had been many wounded people, that they'd had a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic? Sir Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, at the outset, I'm sorry to hear of your injuries. I'm just going to ask you a few questions to attempt to clarify some of the answers you gave us. Do I take, sir, from your name that your ethnicity is that you're a Serb? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm Orthodox, a Serb, and Orthodox by religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted] Was that a civilian function, or at that particular time were you assigned to some military organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. My question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My question, to keep it very simple, is: Was that in a civilian capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And with the outbreak of the conflict, were you required to report to any military organisation and be a part of that, or were you allowed to keep your civilian job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, everybody was given a military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So on the day in question, [redacted] [redacted] is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. On that day, I was a civilian. I did not have a military assignment at all, because I worked throughout that time in hospital, in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On that day, sir, do you know what kind of an incident you were going to with your ambulance? Was it a heart attack or was it someone being shot or was it a car accident? Do you know what you were going to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. I only knew the destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have any clue from the destination as to what type of a call you were responding to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. Until I get there, I can't know what it's all about, so I didn't know who I was going to collect, who I was supposed to collect. He could have been a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you told us about the incident at 4.40 in the morning. I take it -- you said that dawn was just breaking at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes, dawn was breaking. It had already -- it was already light.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: These people that you described, and I don't want to go into any detail, you referred to them as extremists. What do you mean when you use the word "extremists"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Well, I meant by that that all those -- that people, as a group, they can't all be considered to be the same. The ones who were there were extremists, because they were shooting at a clearly-marked ambulance which had a rotation light and an illuminated red cross on the roof, and also red cross markings on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, just a couple more questions. During the months of April or May through to the 5th of August, did you have any involvement with Keraterm in any way, or the facility at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During the months of April through August of 1992, while you were living in Prijedor, were you aware that there was a detention facility at the former Keraterm ceramics facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. I was wounded on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So at no time prior to the 30th of May did you have anything to do with the Keraterm detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: No. I had never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. After the 30th of May, Witness DC, you were in hospital all the time until some 18 months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC
utterances.text: Yes. I was injured on the 30th of May, and on that same day I was taken by plane from Banja Luka to hospitals, where I stayed for 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Witness DC. Do Your Honours have any questions, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know whether I asked whether Your Honours have any questions and whether you replied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You don't. Thank you very much. May the document become a Defence Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We were just discussing that among ourselves. It's not translated, and the relevance is not very evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about Mr. Cirkin in the case, and I'm simply establishing what his present position is. And it's only those two lines that I wish to establish. I don't see the point of having the translators work at several pages of translation if it's only two lines from it which can be dealt by the witness. I'm loath to make translators do anything which is unnecessary, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, it is true that it's just the two lines, but the rest of the document is in a foreign language, and the principle is important. I think we will admit it when it is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I might just address a scheduling matter for today. We're moving along quite quickly. I understand my friend has a potential number of witnesses. I don't know how many he has available today. I just thought I would ask the Court one of two things: It's my understanding that my presence will be required before another Judge on another matter at 4.15 today. I can, of course -- if the Court were to excuse me, my colleague obviously can continue, but I'm just wondering whether or not, in light of the speed with which we are moving, it would be absolutely necessary to -- or whether or not the Court might consider shortened hours for today. I just raise that as an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We were going to make the same request, for this reason: It is extremely difficult for us to go to the prison, if we wish to do so, if we rise at 5.30. In fact, it's impossible. And during the Defence case we do, from time to time, need to take instructions. If possible, we would like to be able to rise, because we're making good progress, at 4.00, if possible, so we can, if necessary, take instructions from our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn at 4.00 this afternoon. Witness DC, that concludes your testimony and you are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're adjourned until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the course of this afternoon, I'm going to be referring with witnesses to a number of documents. I've got copies of the originals and an English translation thereof. The French translation is still in process. Can I give them to you now, please, before the witnesses are called? It seems to make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Some witnesses deal with them more than once. They will be distributed, there are copies for everybody. And that's the English ones. I think the Prosecution has got copies of these documents. I gave a copy to my learned friend this morning, hospital documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yeah. But there is one. I got three copies. Are they three different? I assumed they are two copies --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Three copies of five different documents, I think. Thank you very much. I call, when Mr. Usher is ready, Rajko Vignjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The three documents in the English version I'm going to be referring to are the third, fourth and fifth in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where in the witness summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Your Honour, I didn't realise that's what you meant. 9279, top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Vignjevic, would you be so kind as to tell us your full names, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Rajko Vignjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Vignjevic, were you employed in the general hospital at Prijedor from 1976 onwards and are you still so employed there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you presently work there as a personnel officer?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In May 1992, were you working at the hospital as normal?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in June 1992, were you transferred to the job of warehouseman at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: It wasn't in June. It was in late May of 1992. That is -- that is when I was transferred to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what was your job at the warehouse? Did you have more than one warehouse to look after?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. That was a warehouse which consisted of several units; a food unit, technical equipment unit, then a protection -- protective equipment, electric supplies and so on. I was in charge of all the units except the one for food. In other words, anything that was -- that had to do with technical equipment of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the course of your duties as a warehouseman in the summer of 1992, were there occasions when items were donated by people from outside the hospital, that were brought to your warehouses?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. There were gifts, not only from the town of Prijedor, but from other places too, and in addition to that there was humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when such items were received, were records kept of those items and their receipt?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. There was a rule that whenever a gift would be received by the warehouse, it had to be processed, and the procedure consisted of first -- the gift that was intended would first be inspected, examined by a commission, and then the gift-giver would be present with the commission, and he would be present when the entry was made, and the chief of the warehouse - in this case it was myself - we would all be present when it was entered and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at two documents, please. And if Madam Registrar could give him one from the -- no. It's the original versions, please. One from the pile labelled 3 and one from the pile labelled 5, please. In the English translation, it's the third and fifth pages. If Mr. Usher just gives him one copy, that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend is on his feet, and I hope that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm just hoping that there might be a copy of the original as well for us to look at. Apparently it's a handwritten document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Partly handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would be grateful to have at least a look at that document. Even though I had the translation, I'd like to see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course. There should be a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you want a copy of the original or the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't need the original; just a copy of the original so I can see what the original looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There are two documents, in fact. There's a second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Vignjevic, you're looking at the first document which was given to you. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that's the one which originally was numbered 3 in the bundle. Can you tell us, what is that document exactly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: The document that I'm holding in my hand right now is issued from the previous document. This is the entry -- document reflecting the entry of the gift to the warehouse, and it was drafted on a previous document registering the gift and its receipt at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please: It's signed, I think, at the bottom. Whose signature is that at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: In the document that I'm holding in my hand, it is my signature. This is my signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the other document, please, which is to your left. Again, have a look at that document, please, and then would you be so kind as to tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: This document is the initial document on the receipt of a gift for the hospital. This was compiled by the commission which received it and it is reflected in the signature block, and it describes the article. My signature on this document is not the same as the one on the previous document, but I vary my signature. Sometimes it's a full, sometimes it's a shortened. But it is my signature in both cases, except that in this case it is abbreviated and in the other one it was a full signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And to what item did those two documents relate?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: They refer to the same item, the same article, which is a machine for cleaning of floors, which the person had turned over to the hospital as a gift. It is the same article. But the document reflects the examination of it by the commission, and the other one its entry into the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Mr. Vignjevic, can you recall, please, who was it who physically brought that item to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: This item was delivered by car. I think it was either a van or a small pick-up truck that delivered it, and it was delivered by Dusko Sikirica, with another man who was driving when the item was brought in. He turned it over to the commission for examination and then, later on, it was placed in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And looking at the two documents, they are dated the 1st of August 1992. Was it on the 1st of August 1992 that the item was delivered to the hospital by Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. That was the date of the delivery and when the item was received, that machine, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to August 1992, had you known Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. The acquaintance was not very close but we knew each other. He is from the same neighbourhood, and when we would see each other, we would just greet one another. That was it. We did know one another, not very well, but we were acquainted with one another. Before the war, that is, we had known each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And how long before the war had you known him?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, let's see, perhaps three or four years. I cannot be more precise, but I saw him -- I used to see him three to four years before the war. We are of two different generations so we didn't know each other well, but we did see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to the delivery of the machine to the hospital on the 1st of August, had you seen Dusko Sikirica around the hospital at all?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. I first noticed Dusko, I think this was towards the end of July, around 27, 28. That is when I saw him in the police uniform. At that time, he was part of the security for the hospital. That is when I saw him, and again, not every day but occasionally and subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you see him more than once a day or just once a day? Can you help us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, it would happen that he was on his shift wherever that -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whenever that was, but sometimes I wouldn't see him for an entire day but I would see him the next day. I didn't pay that much attention to that either. I think that he was part of security and -- but I wasn't really paying attention on when he was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in relation to the date of delivery of the machine, for how long after that did you continue to see Dusko Sikirica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: It is hard to say accurately, but I did see him occasionally. It may have been a block of about a month to month and maybe two -- one to two weeks, following the day when he brought the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you wait there, please, Mr. Vignjevic, and answer any questions that may be put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan? Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've been working in that warehouse since 1976; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were transferred to the warehouse in May of 1992, but you'd been working at the hospital since 1976?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And between May of 1992 and the present date, I take it you must have received a lot of equipment and a lot of machines from time to time during the course of your employment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what "many" is. I did receive some. There were gifts, not that many, but if you -- in comparison, there was a lot more humanitarian aid, that is, during the period when I worked in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, my point is it wasn't a particularly momentous occasion for you on the date when the floor polisher arrived, was it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No, no, because it was usual, almost every other day, sometimes two items would arrive of gifts or humanitarian aid, so in that sense, it was usual. I did not pay any special attention to this particular piece of equipment or any other, because there were similar items that came in either before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And, sir, the incident that you're being asked to testify about now is about nine years ago, give or take a month or two?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nodding your head meaning "yes." Sir, do you recall when it was that you were first approached and asked to think back about when it was that you received -- you received the floor polisher in the course of your duties? When was it that you were first approached by anyone to give evidence about this case?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: I was approached to give evidence in this case about perhaps three, three and a half months ago, three to four months ago, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that when you were first approached about this incident, you had no specific recollection about this specific floor polisher being delivered by anyone, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I did remember that the equipment, that this particular equipment -- in fact, this particular piece of equipment is still in our warehouse at the hospital, and when I was asked about it, I immediately said that I did remember, but I did not recall any further details until I went to the archive and I found the record and the entry, and that sort of illuminated me a little bit more, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, let's just analyse what you did remember when you were first asked, sir. You remembered that the floor polisher was around and that you had received it sometime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Until you looked at the documentation in the archives, is it fair to say that you had no specific recollection about who brought it or when it was brought or the exact date when it was brought?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: You could say that in respect of the date, but I immediately recalled who it was that brought it, that had brought it, because I knew that person from before, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I do, but I'm suggesting to you, sir, that it wasn't until you looked at the document which had Dusko Sikirica's name on it that you remembered that it was him. That's how you recognise: Yes, I know that guy.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No. No. As soon as I was asked whether a machine had been brought to the hospital in early August, I said, "Yes, a machine was brought in. It was a floor polisher." And I knew that Dusko Sikirica brought it in a TAM truck. But I said that I would check it in the archives, look in the records of the commission. But I remembered immediately that it was Dusko who brought it, because most of the donors that gave donations and came three or four times are people I remembered. Maybe I don't remember their names, because -- I did know these other people from before the war, but I did know Dusko better than I knew the other donors, and I didn't know that Dusko might -- well, it wasn't he who gave the gift; it was Mr. Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So during the course of your employment, of all the items that you received at the warehouse on a daily or twice-daily basis, you happen to recall that the floor polisher that you were being asked about some nine years later was brought to you by Mr. Sikirica before you looked at the records. Is that what you're asking us to believe, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I recalled because the machine was unusual, because it was unusual and it was big and we didn't have a machine of that kind in the hospital, and it was very useful. So when I thought of that machine, I immediately recalled who had brought it, and I recalled immediately it was Dusko. Because I wish to mention: Maybe I wouldn't have remembered that if I hadn't known Dusko from before. I don't know what might have happened, but it's probably because I knew Dusko from before. So I said, "Oh, yes, I remember it was Dusko who brought it," and then I checked all this in the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, from the documents that have been shown to you, is it fair to say that these certificates, these documents, weren't shown to you before the 11th of December of 2000; it would be sometime since the 11th of December 2000?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, counsel for Mr. Sikirica showed you some pieces of paper in your language. Those documents that you were shown, did you also see a document from the general hospital in Prijedor signed by the director, Radojka Elenkov? Were you shown that document? Were you shown that document by the counsel?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, no. I can't remember that. I know we only talked about the machine. I remembered who had brought the machine in. I didn't remember the date, and I told the lawyer immediately that there must be documentation about this donation. And later on I found these documents and convinced myself that -- well, as for Radojka Elenkov, I can't remember. I don't remember. Goran Elenkov -- Radojka, I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let's not worry about that any longer, sir, because I'm going to ask you a couple of other questions. You were approached and asked about your recollection about the delivery of this machine and then you went back and looked in the records; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Before I looked in the records, before I went to look at them, I remembered the machine, and I remembered the person who had brought the machine in, and it was only then that I went to confirm this in my own mind. I didn't know the exact date, but when I checked the documentation, then I saw what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you given any assistance, sir, in terms of a possible date to commence your search? Were you told that you should maybe look at your search to be around a particular date, like the 1st of August? Were you told?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, no. You know, this is in a file, and I went through the year 1992. You can go through this very fast, and so leafing through these documents, I came upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So let me just see if I get your evidence correctly, sir. You made a totally independent search and you weren't given any assistance from anyone, including the people who were asking you to check, as to a time frame that might be helpful for you to look at?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, they only mentioned the machine, the people I talked to, the lawyers, and then I said I would check it. They asked me for the documents because they wanted to see it and they wanted to see when this was. And I repeat now that I looked through the file, and I was assisted by my associates from the bookkeeping department who keep this file in their office. And so we found it and then we showed it to the Defence counsel, and the record and the entry, all that. I mean, we couldn't do that before I looked and saw whether we had the documents, but I did remember both the machine and the person who brought it in, and then I checked this and confirmed it in my own mind when I saw the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, that's a very long answer to a very simple question. Let me rephrase my question to see whether or not you will agree or disagree with me. Is it your evidence that you were given no assistance by anyone in terms of the time frame for you to look for the date that this receipt may have been written?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did assist, but it was my people from the filing department, the bookkeeping department, who helped me, because they have to make an entry as to the value of every donation, and then a colleague of mine told me that she thought it was late July or early August. And because these records are kept in files according to number, and I pulled out the file and leafed through it, and I didn't want to open it in the middle and try to find July, August at once. I went through from the beginning. But I did get assistance from that colleague of mine, because she was doing the bookkeeping end, the value of the machine, entering it in the books, and she said that she remembered that it was late July or early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me try it one more time. Did counsel for Sikirica, or anyone working on behalf of Mr. Sikirica's defence, give you assistance with respect to a particular date when you might concentrate your search?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I really think he's answered this question about twice now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. With respect, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: His answer was, "They only mentioned the machine, the people I talked to, the lawyers, and then I said I would check it." That, in our submission, is an answer to the question he is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect, at line 0802, as a result of my question, "Did anyone give you any assistance?" he says, "Yes, yes, they did assist. But it was my people from the filing department who helped me," et cetera. I'm now asking for clarification by what he means by "they did assist." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did people from the Defence team assist you in concentrating your search to a particular date? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, do I understand your evidence correctly that you're not really sure just how long it was that you knew Mr. Sikirica before the armed conflict? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you're not sure about the date when you saw him in a police uniform around the hospital either, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: That, well, I saw Sikirica wearing a police uniform in late June. It was the 27th of July, rather, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that you can now recall that you saw him at the hospital in a police uniform on the 27th or 28th of July? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, you see, the 27th of July is -- a traditional event takes place near Prijedor on the 27th of July, and it's an event I usually attend. I always go to these traditional events. A gathering. And it was then that I was about to go to that gathering. So that day sticks in my memory because it's an annual event. So it was the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But that was a date before the delivery of the machine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you say that he was there in a police uniform, and you saw him from time to time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You only assume he was there for the security of the hospital; isn't that true? You didn't -- he didn't tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No. I wasn't told that he was there, but everyone -- that's what people said. I didn't ask anyone, nor did anyone tell me of their own accord, but people said that those people in police uniforms were providing security for the hospital, and so I assume, because he was wearing a police uniform and I saw him that day, I assume that he was working on security, because as hospital employees, we were never given a document which said that somebody was in the security. But seeing someone in a police uniform, of course one assumed he was in the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct. So that's an assumption that you drew from the fact that someone in a police uniform was at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't just he. Others. Would you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me rephrase -- let me ask a couple of others ones, sir. He didn't tell you he was there on police security. It's an assumption you made from the fact that you saw someone in a police uniform there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You don't know, for example, if he was there bringing a prisoner from the Keraterm detention camp for treatment. That's a possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, but if a policeman were to bring an inmate to the hospital, that would be another explanation for seeing him there, other than the fact that he's hospital security?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: But you see, bringing a patient in, that was the entrance on the opposite side of the hospital, and I was working in the basement on the other side of the hospital. The entrance was on the other side. So if someone brought in a patient, it wouldn't be something I would see or know about, the arrival of any patients or anyone. But the building was secured by policemen, and we noticed those policemen at the entrance where I was, and that is why I assumed that was the hospital security at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, did your records disclose to you who the donor of this machine was?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mesanovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you tell, sir, whether or not that is a Croat or Serb or Muslim name? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, the last name is a Muslim one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was it -- did you receive many donations from Muslims at that time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: I wouldn't say we received many, but there were some smaller ones, and bigger ones as well, like that machine. But we didn't receive much from Muslims; not so much from Serbs either. It was from people of other nationalities. There wasn't a lot of that, either from one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you not consider it strange, sir, that an item like that would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be brought to you by someone in a police uniform as opposed to by the donor personally?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Well, maybe it seems strange to me only now. At that time, I didn't think about it, about that strange situation. Other Muslims made donations, they made small gifts, so did Serbs, and they didn't appear odd to me because I thought it was a gift to the hospital. I don't know how, why. But anyway, it was brought in, it was handed in, it was a donation, and I was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It was a donation purportedly from a Muslim individual brought to you by the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Dusko drove it to us in a truck, yes. The Muslim donated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you confirm with the donor that this was a voluntary gift, or whether it was appropriated? Did you do any follow-up when you received this material?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No, I didn't check. I did not establish whether it was voluntary, because I felt that it was a gift for the hospital. Otherwise, it wouldn't be there. It wouldn't be in the hospital. Anyway, it was my job to receive the donation, whoever brought it there. I couldn't refuse a gift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you could, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: And I don't know how it was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I just have one more question, you'll be happy to know. The hospital, just how far is it away from the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Two and a half, three kilometres, two kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So someone could come and go between the two places on a number of times in one day without any difficulty?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. That's my question of you. I'm not suggesting -- is it your evidence --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he could, during the day. Two kilometres is -- it's -- you can go that distance on foot, if need be, in a quarter of an hour. If you go both ways, it's half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Vignjevic, on the occasions during the period of time you've described during which you saw Dusko Sikirica at the hospital, was it always at the side of the hospital where you were working as opposed to the entrance where patients were brought in?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: No. From time to time, I saw him on my side, at my entrance, or rather, in front. Occasionally, not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what was he doing when you saw him at your side of the building?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO Vignjevic
utterances.text: He was just walking around, patrolling around the gate. He would go around, he would walk off. Whether he was going to the other entrance, I don't know, but from my office I could see through the window when a policeman passed around the perimeter. So I don't know whether he went this way or that way. I didn't pay attention. But I would see him there in front. I'm talking about the gate leading to my part of the building, to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Do Your Honours have any questions of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Mr. Vignjevic, that concludes your testimony and you are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder whether the two items which he has identified may acquire exhibit numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I call now Radenko Djervida. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would my friend mind repeating the name? I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you give me a minute? It's Radenko Djervida. It's 9277 in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, apparently my presence is required before another Judge at this particular time. May I please be excused? My colleague will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Djervida, would you please tell us your full names.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Radenko Djervida.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is your date of birth the 21st of September, 1957, are you a resident of Prijedor, and are you of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I'm a resident of Prijedor and I am of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From 1982, were you employed at the general hospital in Prijedor, and did you work there as the manager of the technical services?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I have been employed at the Prijedor hospital since 1982, and I still am today, and I am one of the managers of the technical services.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you occupy that position in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document, please, if you will. It's document labelled number 4 of the originals bundle and it's the fourth page of the English translations.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Djervida: What is that document that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: This is the document recording that I received a certain machine and a certain liquid from Dusko Sikirica, and I signed the receipt with my full name, first name and last name, and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what event was it that caused you to create that document?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, for every item, we always draw up a written document. This is evidence that something arrived in the hospital, both this machine and other types of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when such an item is received in the hospital, what is the procedure by which it is, as it were, brought into the hospital's inventory? What documentation has to be created?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, the basic document is this one, and this is evidence that Dusko Sikirica handed over this machine; and I, as the responsible person from the technical service, received it. All other goods are also delivered with documents, with waybills.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now, we can see there that the first item listed is a machine for the cleaning and polishing of floors. Do you recall that item in particular?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what is it about that item in particular that makes you recall it nine years later?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, it was an important piece of equipment, because we have 20.000 square metres of hospital floor and it had to be cleaned, and it was wartime and many people did not turn up for work, and it was of great help to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to the receipt of this particular machine, had you had a similar size machine or had you had a machine that was of a different size for the floor cleaning? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: We had something, but it was a small machine, not very efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did the receipt of this machine improve the situation as far as floor cleaning in the hospital was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, it did, as I said, because we had 20.000 square metres of surface there, so we needed fewer people involved in cleaning and less supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what was the date upon which you received this machine from Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: As it is stated here, on the 1st of August. I can add that it was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The person from whom you received the machine, Dusko Sikirica, was he somebody that you had known from before the war?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I had not known him before the war. I didn't live in Prijedor. I lived in Gradina. But I would see him during the war. We were not personally acquainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you see him -- apart from this occasion, the 1st of August, 1992, did you see him on other occasions at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I did, following that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Had you seen him at the hospital prior to the occasion on which you received the machine from him?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him before that day too, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And whereabouts in the hospital? What part of the hospital did you see him in before you received the machine?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I would see him at the entrance. Also there was a police platoon that provided security for the hospital, so I saw him around the hospital too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when you saw him around the hospital, what was it that he was doing?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: There was a police platoon. I don't know how many men. They provided security for the hospital, at the entrance, the hallways. It was wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was he part of that police platoon?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Focusing for a moment on the period before you received the machine from him, how long before you received the machine from him did you first see him at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: A couple of times, like the others. I did not pay very much attention to the police presence. I was focusing on my job which was technical services, but in passing, I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What I was after, Mr. Djervida, was the period of time before the machine was brought to the hospital. How long before that machine was brought in did you first see Dusko Sikirica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many days; maybe up to ten, seven, eight. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And after the machine was received, how long did you continue to see him at the hospital; for what period?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, several times when I would come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And how long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I think throughout August, the police was there for the security of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, would you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No cross-examination? Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've indicated that during this period before the machine was brought to the hospital, that you saw Mr. Sikirica at the hospital a couple of times, "like the others," you said. What others are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I said the police platoon. I don't know their number but they provided security for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You also said that you were engaged in your own work at that time, and that you didn't pay much attention to what he's doing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Correct, because there was no power, there was no water, and we had to keep the hospital running.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. And when was it that you were first asked to cast your mind back to 1992, and in particular, to the whereabouts of Mr. Sikirica at that time? When were you first asked to think back to 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Nobody asked me. I remembered. The machine is still at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, but did somebody approach you and ask you something about the machine or something about Mr. Sikirica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, yes. The Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in January or February.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: January or February of this year?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And when you were approached, were you shown these documents that record the date on which the machine was received as being the 1st of August 1992? Were you shown those documents?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And it's those documents that you base your recollection on? That is, it's that date that's recorded on the document from which you conclude that you saw Mr. Sikirica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. I also have it in my agenda as an entry, as all other significant things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What exactly is your agenda?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: It's an agenda book where I noted down all important things then, as I have continued to do to date, regarding business.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So it's another document that records the machine as having been brought on the 1st of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, my personal note.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So it's possible that, in terms of the period after the machine was brought, that Mr. Sikirica wasn't at the hospital until, say, after the 5th of August. That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I don't know. It doesn't seem possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Why doesn't it seem possible, given that your recollection is based upon the document that records the machine as having been brought to the hospital on the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I don't understand exactly what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that your recollection of having seen Mr. Sikirica at the hospital is based entirely upon the documents that you were shown and your agenda that records this floor polisher as having been received by Mr. Sikirica on the 1st of August, 1992. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, yes. On the basis of my notes and of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So therefore you have no independent recollection - that's apart from the documents - as to the date or dates upon which you saw Mr. Sikirica at the hospital. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I do remember, of course I do, because we tested the machine in front of him. We tested it to see whether it was in working order or not. Of course I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And that was on the 1st of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let's focus on what you can remember for the moment, and again I'll suggest to you that your memory as to when Mr. Sikirica was at the hospital is based entirely upon those documents which record the date upon which he brought the machine as being the 1st of August. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I agree that it is both in the document and in my note. We spent a certain time there testing it and everything else. We didn't just receive it without checking it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. But it's possible, isn't it, that in terms of this month that you saw him working at the hospital, that it was sometime, say, after the 5th of August? That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: It's impossible. The document is dated 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You have no independent recollection of seeing him on any other particular date. You follow?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: I indeed do not understand what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: You have no other documents which you can use to refresh your memory as to when he was there, that is, apart from the documents in relation to the floor polisher. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. No other documents. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And so I suggest to you that you're assuming that he was there for the month or so after the 1st of August only because you have that document.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. There is a document, there's my note in the agenda book, and the memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You, as you've quite fairly said, were involved with your own duties, and so you weren't paying a great deal of attention to what Mr. Sikirica was doing when he was at the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And Keraterm camp is some two kilometres away from the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Can you help me about this, please, just so that we're clear: The document that's been referred to in the English language as your agenda, is that what we would think of as a diary, with entries for each day of the month and each day of the year?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: You mean my agenda book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Just describe -- is that a book which contains, like a diary, entries for each day and date of the year?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. It was my personal agenda book or diary, and because we had the sequence of events moving along very fast, I needed to keep notes. Because of the shortages of power and water, for instance, for the dialysis purposes and things like that, I had to keep all these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you've described this book as being one where you put notes about important events. Is it the position that the arrival of this machine fell into the category of important events requiring you or motivating you to make an entry in your agenda?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it, as you have described, those documents and your memory which enable you to say that thereafter you continued to see Dusko Sikirica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO DJERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Do Your Honours have any questions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May he be released, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Djervida, that concludes your testimony and you are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And may the document acquire an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Dusko Coric, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: 9280, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, would you please tell us your full names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Dusko Coric, 1st of March, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And do you live in Prijedor and are you of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I live in Prijedor and I'm of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you worked at Prijedor general hospital since 1986?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And from 1987, were you working there as a warehouse clerk?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us about this, please: The people who were working in your section, were they drawn from all the ethnic backgrounds that existed in Prijedor before the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is that a situation which continued throughout the summer months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: The interethnic relations were all right until the interethnic conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The question which I asked you and which I'd like you to deal with, please: Did the people from different ethnic backgrounds, did they continue to work at the hospital throughout the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Not all the summer. I don't remember, but they started leaving on their own in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to May 1992, did you know Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long had you known him prior to May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: I've known him for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And how did you come to know him? Was he someone who lived near you, or was he a friend or at school with you? How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: He lived near me and we went to school together; not the same class but same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would you call yourself an acquaintance or a friend or a good friend? How would you describe your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Dusko is a very good pal, a friend, like ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me about this: Was one of the duties you had as a warehouse clerk involved in receiving items that had been donated from persons outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May he look, please, at D31 and D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at these two documents, Mr. Coric, and when you've looked at them, tell us what they are, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: This is a gift that Dusko Sikirica delivered to our hospital as a gift from Mr. Smail Mesanovic. It was a machine for floor cleaning, including tile cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you present when Mr. Sikirica brought that machine to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Prior to that machine being brought to the hospital -- and I think the date on there is the 1st of August. Prior to the 1st of August, had you seen Dusko Sikirica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Dule started working as -- on security, I think, on the 27th, on the security of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when he started working on the security of the building, did you see him, and indeed did you speak to him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Not much, just exchanged greeting on -- as I was arriving to work. It was all done, just fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In which area of the hospital did you see him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to the hospital. They were sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when you spoke to him, did you establish with him what his duties at the hospital were?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: To provide security for the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And after the 27th of July, did you continue to see him on a daily basis or weekly basis? Can you help us about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Not on a daily basis. They worked in shifts until, I think, the end of August, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is there any indication on the two documents you've got in front of you that it was Dusko Sikirica who was recorded as having brought the item to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there is his signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After the 1st of August, did you continue to see him in the same place at the hospital or was he engaged in duties elsewhere in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: In the lobby, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you see him in the days immediately following the delivery of the machine?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And until when did you continue to see Dusko Sikirica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, sometime towards the close of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when you saw him in the lobby, what was he doing in the lobby?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Where the duty officers were sitting, in a chair or at the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you visit the lobby frequently as part of your duties or go through it frequently, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Every day, every morning when I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you speak with Dusko on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly, I would just say, "Hello, what's new?" And then I would hurry on to work because I had a lot to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you spend -- if I can just deal with your knowledge of Dusko Sikirica before the war, would you spend time, as it were, in social situations with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Would you spend time with him? For example, would you go to a bar with him or to a cafe or out to dinner with him or visit his home? That's what I mean by meeting him in a social setting.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: You mean before the war? Before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Before the war, well, no. Well, he had his friends and I had mine, but we were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you able to observe him in the company with people from other ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what impression did you form of how he dealt with, got on with, people who weren't Serb? In other words, the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: They would have a drink together, joke around, keep company together, and so on. Not just he, but everyone; people of different ethnic backgrounds socialised before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And as to his personal character, would you describe him as extrovert, outgoing, noisy, or introvert, quiet and retiring? How would you describe him?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO CORIC
utterances.text: He was quiet but he liked to joke. But he was quiet. He -- he didn't push himself forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I probably will be some time with this witness. I don't know whether Your Honour wishes to adjourn for the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn. Mr. Coric, we are going to take the adjournment for the afternoon. We will resume at 9.30 in the morning. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes the members of the Defence. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 4.06 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday the 28th day of June, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 25
